result: The LPS-HVV two-hit model induces hypoxemia, neutrophil infiltration, increased vascular permeability, and NETs formation in mice. The combination of LPS and high-volume ventilation (HVV) caused significant reduction in arterial PaO2, increased neutrophil migration, albumin leakage, IL-1β, and NETs markers (MPO, NE, histone-DNA, MPO-DNA complexes) in BALF.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm the model and findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the data are convincing,' Reviewer 2 notes the authors 'proved that IL1R1 is involved in ALI model,' and Reviewer 3 states the authors 'demonstrate quite convincingly' the role of IL-1β in this model. No concerns were raised about the LPS-HVV model or the characterization of hypoxemia and NETs formation.

result: Neutrophil depletion prevents hypoxemia and reduces lung injury markers in the LPS-HVV model. Depletion with anti-Ly6G antibody prevented hypoxemia, reduced albumin and IL-6 in BALF, and decreased MPO, NE, and NETs formation, without affecting IL-1β or TNFα levels.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without critique. Reviewer 3 notes the authors use 'a variety of in vivo animal-based and in vitro cell culture work, and interventions including global gene knockout, cell-targeted knockout and pharmacological inhibition, which greatly strengthen the ability to make clear biological interpretations.' The neutrophil depletion data are part of this comprehensive approach and are not questioned.

result: NETs formation is required for hypoxemia in the LPS-HVV model. Neutrophil-specific PAD4 deletion and DNase I treatment both significantly inhibited hypoxemia development and reduced albumin leakage and NETs markers (MPO-DNA complexes), without altering IL-1β levels.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'proved that IL1R1 is involved in ALI model proving that IL1b signalling leads towards ARDS,' and Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'demonstrate quite convincingly that interleukin 1 beta plays a role in the development of ventilator-induced lung injury in this model, and that this role includes the regulation of neutrophil extracellular trap formation.' The PAD4 and DNase I experiments are part of this convincing demonstration.

result: IL-1R1 signaling is critical for hypoxemia and NETs formation in the LPS-HVV model. Il1r1-/- mice did not develop hypoxemia and had reduced NETs, albumin leakage, MPO, NE, and cell death markers compared to wild-type mice.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly support these findings. Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'They used IL1R1 ko mice and proved that IL1R1 is involved in ALI model proving that IL1b signalling leads towards ARDS.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'demonstrate quite convincingly that interleukin 1 beta plays a role in the development of ventilator-induced lung injury in this model.' No concerns were raised about the IL-1R1 knockout data.

result: IL-1β, but not LPS, enhances ionomycin-induced NETs formation in bone marrow neutrophils (BMN) and alveolar neutrophils (AN) in vitro.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the comprehensive demonstration of IL-1β's role in NETs formation. Reviewer 3 states the authors 'demonstrate quite convincingly that interleukin 1 beta plays a role in the development of ventilator-induced lung injury in this model, and that this role includes the regulation of neutrophil extracellular trap formation.' The in vitro data support the in vivo findings and are not questioned.

result: Therapeutic hypothermia (32°C) prevents hypoxemia and reduces lung injury markers in the LPS-HVV model. Hypothermia prevented hypoxemia development and reduced albumin leakage, IL-1β, IL-6, TNFα, MPO, NE, soluble GSDMD, and NETs formation in BALF, without causing alkalosis or acidosis.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm the hypothermia findings. Reviewer 1 states the study provides 'a comprehensive exploration of the role of hypothermia of mitigating IL-1β induction and NETosis in the context of lung injury induced by mechanical ventilation. The data are convincing.' Reviewer 2 notes 'hypothermia reduces this effect, suggesting a therapeutic option.' No concerns were raised about the hypothermia data.

result: Hypothermia inhibits IL-1β release from macrophages through reduced GSDMD expression and cleavage, independent of caspase-1 activation or autophagy. LPS-primed macrophages stimulated at 32°C with ATP or nigericin released less IL-1β and showed reduced GSDMD cleavage compared to 37°C, with accumulation of unreleased mature IL-1β intracellularly.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these mechanistic findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the data are convincing,' and Reviewer 3 notes the authors use 'a variety of in vivo animal-based and in vitro cell culture work' that 'greatly strengthen the ability to make clear biological interpretations.' The GSDMD mechanism is part of this comprehensive approach and is not questioned.

result: Hypothermia (32°C) reduces NETs formation in neutrophils in vitro. Both bone marrow neutrophils (BMN) and alveolar neutrophils (AN) stimulated at 32°C showed significantly reduced NETs formation compared to 37°C.
evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the comprehensive demonstration of hypothermia's effects on NETs formation. Reviewer 1 states the study provides 'a comprehensive exploration of the role of hypothermia of mitigating IL-1β induction and NETosis.' The in vitro neutrophil data support the in vivo findings and are not questioned.

result: Hypothermia modulates NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1β release, and NETs formation, preventing LPS-HVV-induced acute respiratory failure. The authors conclude that IL-1β plays a significant role as a driver of the vicious cycle in ventilation-induced ALI and ARDS, and that the inflammasome pathway and its downstream mediators may be effective therapeutic targets that could be downmodulated by hypothermia.
evaluation: Reviewers affirm these conclusions. Reviewer 1 states 'the study is important for the field.' Reviewer 2 notes 'hypothermia reduces this effect, suggesting a therapeutic option.' Reviewer 3 states the authors 'demonstrate quite convincingly that interleukin 1 beta plays a role in the development of ventilator-induced lung injury in this model.' The overall conclusions are supported by the comprehensive data presented.
